title: Cell Structure & Organelles (NCERT Class 8–9)
answer: The cell is the fundamental structural and functional unit of life, first discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665. Mitochondria generate ATP and are termed the 'powerhouse of the cell', while chloroplasts conduct photosynthesis in plant cells.
highlights: Discovery: Robert Hooke (1665 in cork tissue); Antonie van Leeuwenhoek (first live cells, 1674)
Key Organelles: Nucleus (control center / DNA), Mitochondria (ATP synthesis / Powerhouse), Chloroplast (photosynthesis in plants), Ribosomes (protein synthesis), Lysosomes (suicide bags)
Plant vs Animal: Plant cells have a rigid cellulose cell wall, large central vacuole, and plastids (chloroplasts); animal cells lack cell walls and chloroplasts

title: Plant and Animal Tissues (NCERT Class 9)
answer: Plant tissues are divided into meristematic (dividing) and permanent tissues (complex vascular tissues: Xylem transports water/minerals unidirectionally, Phloem transports food bidirectionally). Animal tissues comprise epithelial, connective (blood, bone, cartilage), muscular, and nervous tissues.
highlights: Xylem: Composed of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma, and xylem fibres; conducts water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves
Phloem: Composed of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres, and phloem parenchyma; translocates sucrose bidirectionally

Animal Tissues: 1) Epithelial (protective covering), 2) Connective (Blood - fluid matrix with RBCs/WBCs/platelets, Bone, Cartilage, Areolar), 3) Muscular (striated, smooth, cardiac), 4) Nervous (neurons)

title: Photosynthesis — Mechanism & Chemical Equation (NCERT Class 7 & 10)
answer: Photosynthesis is the autotrophic process where green plants synthesize glucose and release oxygen from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight absorbed by chlorophyll: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Sunlight → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂.
highlights: Balanced Equation: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + Sunlight (Chlorophyll) → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂

Three Main Steps: 1) Absorption of light energy by chlorophyll, 2) Conversion of light to chemical energy and splitting of water into hydrogen and oxygen (photolysis), 3) Reduction of carbon dioxide to carbohydrates
Site: Chloroplasts (specifically thylakoids for light reactions and stroma for dark/Calvin cycle)

title: Aerobic vs Anaerobic Respiration (NCERT Class 7 & 10)
answer: Aerobic respiration breaks down glucose completely in the presence of oxygen to yield CO₂, H₂O, and 36–38 ATP in mitochondria. Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen in yeast (yielding ethanol + CO₂ + 2 ATP) or in human muscle cells under intense exercise (yielding lactic acid + 2 ATP, causing muscle cramps).
highlights: Aerobic: Glucose → Pyruvate (in cytoplasm) → CO₂ + H₂O + Energy (in mitochondria)
Anaerobic in Yeast: Glucose → Pyruvate → Ethanol + CO₂ + Energy (Fermentation)
Anaerobic in Human Muscle: Glucose → Pyruvate → Lactic Acid + Energy (causes muscle fatigue/cramps)

title: Modes of Reproduction — Asexual & Sexual (NCERT Class 8 & 10)
answer: Asexual reproduction involves a single parent producing genetically identical offspring (Binary fission in Amoeba, Budding in Hydra/Yeast, Regeneration in Planaria, Spore formation in Rhizopus). Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of male and female gametes to produce genetic variation.
highlights: Asexual Modes: Binary Fission (Amoeba, Leishmania), Multiple Fission (Plasmodium), Budding (Hydra, Yeast), Fragmentation (Spirogyra), Vegetative Propagation (Bryophyllum leaf buds, Rose cuttings)
Plant Sexual Reproduction: Pollination (transfer of pollen from anther to stigma) followed by double fertilization forming zygote and endosperm
Human Reproduction: Male gamete (sperm produced in testes) fertilizes female gamete (ovum released from ovary) in the fallopian tube

title: Light: Reflection & Refraction (NCERT Class 10)
answer: The laws of reflection state that the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection (∠i = ∠r). Refraction is the bending of light when transitioning between media, governed by Snell's Law: sin(i) / sin(r) = n (refractive index). Mirror formula is 1/f = 1/v + 1/u, and Lens formula is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
highlights: Mirror Formula: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u (Magnification m = -v/u = h'/h)
Lens Formula: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u (Magnification m = v/u = h'/h)
Power of a Lens: P = 1/f (in metres), expressed in Dioptres (D); Convex lens has +P, Concave lens has -P
Applications: Concave mirror in dentist tools & solar furnaces; Convex mirror as vehicle rear-view mirror (erect, diminished, wide field of view)

title: Electricity & Ohm's Law (NCERT Class 10)
answer: Ohm's Law states that electric current (I) is directly proportional to potential difference (V) at constant temperature: V = I·R. For series resistors R_eq = R₁ + R₂ + ..., while for parallel resistors 1/R_eq = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...
highlights: Ohm's Law: V = IR (Resistance unit: Ohm, Ω)
Resistivity Formula: R = ρ·(l / A) (where ρ is resistivity in Ω·m, l is length, A is cross-sectional area)
Joule's Law of Heating: H = I²Rt (Heat in Joules)
Electric Power: P = VI = I²R = V²/R (Commercial unit of electrical energy: 1 kWh = 1 Unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules)

title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current (NCERT Class 10)
answer: An electric current produces a magnetic field around it, first discovered by Hans Christian Oersted in 1820. The direction of magnetic field lines around a straight current conductor is given by Maxwell's Right-Hand Thumb Rule, while the direction of mechanical force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field is determined by Fleming's Left-Hand Rule.
highlights: Right-Hand Thumb Rule: Thumb points in direction of current; curled fingers give direction of magnetic field lines
Solenoid: A coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wrapped closely in a cylinder; produces uniform internal magnetic field like a bar magnet
Fleming's Left-Hand Rule (Electric Motor): Thumb = Motion/Force, Forefinger = Magnetic Field, Center finger = Current
Fleming's Right-Hand Rule (Electric Generator / Induced Current): Determines direction of induced current from electromagnetic induction

title: Acids, Bases and Salts & pH Scale (NCERT Class 7 & 10)
answer: Acids release H⁺ (or H₃O⁺) ions in aqueous solution and turn blue litmus red (pH < 7). Bases release OH⁻ ions and turn red litmus blue (pH > 7). Neutralization occurs when an acid reacts with a base to form salt and water: Acid + Base → Salt + Water.
highlights: pH Scale: Developed by Soren Sorensen (1909); ranges from 0 (strongly acidic) to 14 (strongly basic), with 7 being neutral (pure water)
Common Indicators: Litmus (Blue to Red in acid), Phenolphthalein (colorless in acid, pink in base), Methyl orange (red in acid, yellow in base)
Important Salts: Bleaching powder (CaOCl₂), Baking soda (NaHCO₃), Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O), Plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O)

title: Metals, Non-Metals & Reactivity Series (NCERT Class 8 & 10)
answer: Metals are electropositive elements characterized by malleability, ductility, high electrical conductivity, and sonority, whereas non-metals are electronegative. The metal reactivity series lists metals in descending order of reactivity: K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > [H] > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au.
highlights: Reactivity Series: Potassium (most reactive) > Sodium > Calcium > Magnesium > Aluminium > Zinc > Iron > Lead > Hydrogen > Copper > Silver > Gold (least reactive)
Exceptions: Mercury is a liquid metal at room temperature; Bromine is a liquid non-metal; Iodine is a lustrous non-metal; Diamond is a non-metal with high melting point and thermal conductivity
Amphoteric Oxides: Metal oxides that react with both acids and bases to produce salt and water (e.g., Al₂O₃, ZnO)

title: Carbon & Its Compounds (NCERT Class 10)
answer: Carbon forms versatile covalent bonds due to tetravalency (valency of 4) and catenation (ability to form long chains with itself). Its main allotropes are diamond (3D tetrahedral lattice), graphite (hexagonal layered lattice), and buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀).
highlights: Two Unique Properties: 1) Catenation (self-linking capability), 2) Tetravalency (forms 4 covalent bonds)
Allotropes: Diamond (hardest natural substance, electrical insulator), Graphite (soft, slippery, good electrical conductor due to free delocalized electrons), Fullerene (C₆₀ football cage)
Functional Groups: Alcohol (-OH), Aldehyde (-CHO), Ketone (-CO-), Carboxylic Acid (-COOH), Halogens (-Cl, -Br)
Homologous Series: Family of organic compounds with same functional group and a constant -CH₂- difference between successive members (14 u mass difference)

title: Human Digestive System & Enzymes (NCERT Class 7 & 10)
answer: The human digestive system consists of the alimentary canal (mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, rectum) and associated glands (salivary glands, liver, pancreas). Salivary amylase begins starch digestion in the mouth, pepsin breaks down proteins in the acidic stomach, and bile emulsifies fats in the alkaline small intestine.
highlights: Mouth: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) digests starch into maltose
Stomach: Gastric glands secrete HCl (kills bacteria, creates acidic pH ~1.5–2.0), Pepsin (digests proteins into peptones), and Mucus (protects stomach lining)
Small Intestine: Site of complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins, and fats; absorbs nutrients via finger-like projections called Villi
Pancreatic Enzymes: Trypsin (digests proteins), Pancreatic amylase (carbohydrates), Lipase (emulsified fats)

title: Human Circulatory System & Double Circulation (NCERT Class 10)
answer: The human heart is a four-chambered muscular organ (two atria and two ventricles) that operates a double circulation system where blood flows through the heart twice during each complete cycle (pulmonary circulation to lungs and systemic circulation to body tissues).
highlights: Four Chambers: Right Atrium (receives deoxygenated blood from body), Right Ventricle (pumps blood to lungs via pulmonary artery), Left Atrium (receives oxygenated blood from lungs via pulmonary vein), Left Ventricle (pumps oxygenated blood to body via aorta)
Double Circulation: Consists of Pulmonary Circulation (Heart → Lungs → Heart) and Systemic Circulation (Heart → Body Tissues → Heart)

Arteries vs Veins: Arteries have thick, elastic walls and carry oxygenated blood away from heart under high pressure (exception: pulmonary artery); Veins have thin walls with valves to prevent backflow and carry deoxygenated blood toward heart (exception: pulmonary vein)
Blood Components: Plasma, RBCs (Hemoglobin carries O₂), WBCs (immunity), Platelets (blood clotting)

title: Human Nervous System, Neurons & Reflex Arc (NCERT Class 10)
answer: The nervous system comprises the Central Nervous System (Brain and Spinal Cord) and Peripheral Nervous System (cranial and spinal nerves). The structural and functional unit of the nervous system is the Neuron, consisting of a cell body (cyton), dendrites, axon, and synapse.
highlights: Neuron Parts: Dendrites (receive chemical signals), Cyton/Cell Body, Axon (transmits electrical nerve impulse), Synapse (microscopic junction between two neurons where neurotransmitters transmit chemical signals)
Reflex Arc: Pathway of automatic, instantaneous involuntary response to a stimulus: Receptor → Sensory Neuron → Relay Neuron in Spinal Cord → Motor Neuron → Effector Muscle

Brain Regions: Forebrain (Cerebrum — thinking, voluntary actions, memory), Midbrain (visual and auditory reflexes), Hindbrain (Cerebellum — posture and balance; Medulla oblongata — involuntary actions like breathing, blood pressure; Pons)

title: Human Excretory System & Nephron (NCERT Class 10)
answer: The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, a pair of ureters, a urinary bladder, and a urethra. The structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney is the Nephron, which filters metabolic nitrogenous waste (urea, uric acid) from the blood.
highlights: Nephron Structure: Bowman's capsule enclosing the Glomerulus (filtration unit), followed by Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT), Loop of Henle, Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT), and Collecting Duct

Three Steps of Urine Formation: 1) Glomerular Ultrafiltration (filters water, glucose, amino acids, salts, urea), 2) Selective Reabsorption (essential glucose, amino acids, and water reabsorbed into capillaries), 3) Tubular Secretion (active secretion of excess ions into filtrate)
Artificial Kidney (Hemodialysis): Device used to clean nitrogenous metabolic wastes from blood in patients with renal failure

title: Ecosystem, Trophic Levels & 10% Energy Law (NCERT Class 10)
answer: An ecosystem consists of biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) and abiotic components (temperature, water, soil). According to Lindeman's 10% Law of Energy Transfer (1942), only about 10% of the energy available at one trophic level is transferred to the next higher level, while 90% is lost as metabolic heat.
highlights: Trophic Levels: Producers (Autotrophs: T1) → Primary Consumers (Herbivores: T2) → Secondary Consumers (Carnivores: T3) → Tertiary Consumers (Apex predators: T4)
Lindeman's 10% Law: If producers capture 10,000 J of solar energy, herbivores receive 1,000 J, primary carnivores receive 100 J, and apex predators receive 10 J
Biological Magnification: Progressive accumulation of non-biodegradable toxic chemicals (like DDT) in higher trophic levels of a food chain
Ozone Layer Depletion: Ozone (O₃) in stratosphere shields Earth from UV-B radiation; depleted by Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), addressed by the 1987 Montreal Protocol

title: Indus Valley Civilization / Harappan Culture (NCERT Class 6 & 12)
answer: The Indus Valley Civilization (c. 2600 – 1900 BCE) was a Bronze Age urban civilization in northwestern South Asia renowned for its advanced town planning, grid street layout, baked-brick architecture, and covered drainage systems. Key sites include Harappa (discovered by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921) and Mohenjo-daro (discovered by RD Banerji in 1922).
highlights: Key Sites: Harappa (Ravi river, Punjab, Pakistan), Mohenjo-daro (Indus river, Sindh — Great Bath, Bronze Dancing Girl, Priest-King), Lothal (Gujarat — artificial dockyard/port), Kalibangan (Rajasthan — ploughed field), Dholavira (Gujarat — water harvesting reservoirs)
Town Planning: Citadel (elevated western public sector) and Lower Town (residential grid system); drainage pipes running beneath streets
Economy & Trade: Traded with Mesopotamia (known as Meluhha in cuneiform texts); standardized stone weights (chert cubical weights based on binary/decimal system)

title: The Vedic Period and Four Vedas
answer: The Vedic Period (~1500–500 BCE) is divided into Early Vedic (Rigvedic, ~1500–1000 BCE) and Later Vedic (~1000–500 BCE). The four Vedas are: Rigveda (oldest, 1,028 hymns), Samaveda (music/chants), Yajurveda (rituals/sacrifices), and Atharvaveda (charms, medicine, spells).
highlights: Rigveda: Oldest religious text, contains Gayatri Mantra (dedicated to Savitr)
Upanishads: Philosophical commentaries (108 total); Satyameva Jayate taken from Mundaka Upanishad
Early Vedic society was pastoral and egalitarian; Sabha and Samiti were popular assemblies
Later Vedic saw rise of Janapadas, iron usage (Krishna Ayas), and rigid Varna system

title: Mauryan Empire & Emperor Ashoka (NCERT Class 6 & 12)
answer: The Mauryan Empire (322 – 185 BCE) was founded by Chandragupta Maurya with the strategic counsel of Chanakya (Kautilya, author of the Arthashastra). Its greatest emperor, Ashoka the Great (ruled c. 268–232 BCE), renounced war following the catastrophic Kalinga War (261 BCE) and adopted Buddhism and Dhamma.
highlights: Capital: Pataliputra (modern Patna, Bihar)
Founder: Chandragupta Maurya (defeated the Nanda dynasty and Seleucus I Nicator; Megasthenes wrote 'Indica')
Ashoka's Edicts: Inscribed in Prakrit (Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts), Greek, and Aramaic on rock faces and polished monolithic sandstone pillars across the subcontinent
Emblem of India: The Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath was adopted as the National Emblem of India on 26 January 1950

title: Gupta Empire — Golden Age of Ancient India (320–550 CE)
answer: The Gupta Empire (320–550 CE) founded by Sri Gupta and consolidated by Chandragupta I, Samudragupta (Napoleon of India), and Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), is known as the Golden Age of India for revolutionary achievements in science, mathematics, astronomy, and Sanskrit literature.
highlights: Samudragupta: Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar inscription by Harisena) records his unbroken conquests
Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya): Court had Navratnas including great poet Kalidasa and physician Dhanvantari
Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya): Computed π ≈ 3.1416, proposed Earth rotates on axis and eclipses are shadows
Ajanta cave paintings and Mehrauli Iron Pillar (rustless metallurgy) belong to this era

title: Mughal Empire — Akbar, Shah Jahan & Governance (NCERT Class 7)
answer: The Mughal Empire was founded in India by Babur after defeating Ibrahim Lodi in the First Battle of Panipat (1526). Its greatest ruler, Jalal-ud-din Muhammad Akbar (ruled 1556–1605), established a centralized administrative framework (Mansabdari and Todar Mal's Zabt revenue systems) and promoted religious tolerance (Sulh-i-Kul).
highlights: Key Emperors: Babur (1526–1530) → Humayun (1530–1556) → Akbar (1556–1605) → Jahangir (1605–1627) → Shah Jahan (1628–1658) → Aurangzeb (1658–1707)

Akbar's Reforms: Abolished Jizya tax on non-Muslims, established Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri, formulated synthetic religious philosophy 'Din-i-Ilahi' (1582), and instituted Navratnas (Birbal, Tansen, Todar Mal, Abul Fazl)
Shah Jahan's Architecture: Golden age of Mughal architecture — built Taj Mahal (UNESCO World Heritage Site), Red Fort, and Jama Masjid in Delhi
Aurangzeb: Re-imposed Jizya, expanded empire to maximum geographic extent across Deccan, faced intense resistance from Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj

keywords: directive principles of state policy dpsp
title: Indian Constitution — Fundamental Rights & Governance (NCERT Class 8–10)
answer: The Constitution of India was drafted by the Constituent Assembly under Drafting Committee Chairman Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and came into effect on 26 January 1950. Part III guarantees six Fundamental Rights (Articles 12–35) protected by constitutional remedies under Article 32.
highlights: Six Fundamental Rights: 1) Right to Equality (Arts. 14–18), 2) Right to Freedom (Arts. 19–22), 3) Right against Exploitation (Arts. 23–24), 4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Arts. 25–28), 5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Arts. 29–30), 6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Art. 32 — termed 'Heart and Soul of Constitution' by Ambedkar)
Directive Principles (DPSP): Part IV (Articles 36–51) borrowed from the Irish Constitution; non-justiciable guidelines for establishing a welfare state
Fundamental Duties: Part IV-A (Article 51A) added by 42nd Amendment (1976) on recommendations of Swaran Singh Committee (11 duties today)
Preamble: Declares India to be a 'Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic'

title: Types of Rocks & The Rock Cycle (NCERT Class 7 & 11)
answer: Rocks are classified into three major groups based on their mode of formation: Igneous (formed by cooling and solidification of magma/lava, e.g., granite, basalt), Sedimentary (formed by deposition and lithification of mineral sediments, e.g., sandstone, limestone), and Metamorphic (formed by alteration of existing rocks under intense heat and pressure, e.g., marble, slate).
highlights: Igneous Rocks (Primary Rocks): Intrusive (cools slowly underground forming large crystals, e.g., Granite) and Extrusive (cools rapidly on surface, e.g., Basalt of Deccan Traps)
Sedimentary Rocks: Layered strata containing fossils and fuel deposits (Sandstone, Limestone, Shale, Coal)
Metamorphic Rocks: Limestone transforms into Marble; Sandstone transforms into Quartzite; Clay/Shale transforms into Slate/Schist
Rock Cycle: Continuous geological transformation of rocks through melting, cooling, weathering, sedimentation, and metamorphism

title: Major Rivers of India — Himalayan & Peninsular Systems (NCERT Class 9)
answer: India's drainage is divided into Himalayan rivers (perennial, snow-fed: Ganga, Indus, Brahmaputra) and Peninsular rivers (seasonal, rain-fed: Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri, Mahanadi flowing east into Bay of Bengal; Narmada, Tapi flowing west into Arabian Sea).
highlights: Ganga (2,525 km): Originates as Bhagirathi from Gangotri Glacier (Gaumukh); joins Alaknanda at Devprayag; forms Sundarbans Delta with Brahmaputra
Indus (3,180 km): Originates near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet; major tributaries: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej (Panjnad)
Brahmaputra (2,900 km): Originates as Tsangpo in Tibet; enters India in Arunachal Pradesh as Dihang; contains world's largest inhabited river island Majuli (Assam)
Godavari (1,465 km): Known as 'Dakshin Ganga' (Ganges of the South) and Vriddha Ganga; longest peninsular river originating at Trimbakeshwar (Maharashtra)
West-Flowing Rivers: Narmada (originates at Amarkantak) and Tapi flow through rift valleys into the Arabian Sea without forming deltas (form estuaries)

keywords: alluvial soil black soil red soil laterite soil
title: Major Soil Types of India (NCERT Class 10)
answer: India features six major soil groups mapped by ICAR: Alluvial soil (most widespread and fertile, 40% area in northern plains), Black soil (Regur soil, rich in clay, ideal for cotton cultivation in Deccan Traps), Red and Yellow soil, Laterite soil (leached soil ideal for tea, coffee, cashew), Arid/Desert soil, and Forest/Mountain soil.
highlights: Alluvial Soil: Deposited by Himalayan rivers; divided into Khadar (new, fine, highly fertile flood plain soil) and Bhangar (older, coarser alluvial soil with kankar nodules)
Black Soil (Regur): Formed by weathering of basaltic lava in Deccan Plateau (Maharashtra, Gujarat, MP); self-aerating with high moisture retention; optimal for cotton
Laterite Soil: Formed in areas of high temperature and heavy rainfall due to intense leaching; rich in iron oxide and aluminium; ideal for plantation crops (tea, coffee, rubber)
Soil Conservation Techniques: Contour ploughing, terrace farming, strip cropping, and shelter belts

title: Major Cropping Seasons & Crops of India (NCERT Class 10)
answer: India has three distinct cropping seasons: Kharif (sown in June–July with monsoon onset and harvested in September–October: Rice, Maize, Jowar, Bajra, Cotton, Jute), Rabi (sown in winter October–December and harvested in April–June: Wheat, Barley, Mustard, Gram, Peas), and Zaid (short summer season March–June: Watermelon, Cucumber, Vegetables).
highlights: Kharif Season: Monsoon crops (Rice/Paddy is the chief food crop of India, requiring high heat >25°C and rainfall >100 cm)
Rabi Season: Winter crops (Wheat requires cool growing season and bright sunshine at harvest; 50–75 cm annual rainfall; Punjab, Haryana, UP leading producers)
Cash / Commercial Crops: Sugarcane (UP leading), Cotton (Black soil of Gujarat/Maharashtra), Tea (Assam leading), Coffee (Karnataka leading)

title: Indian Parliament (Sansad) — Structure & Functions (NCERT Class 8)
answer: The Parliament of India (Sansad) is the supreme bicameral legislative body comprising the President of India, the Lok Sabha (House of the People / Lower House, 543 elected MPs), and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States / Upper House, 250 members: 238 elected from states/UTs and 12 nominated by the President).
highlights: Lok Sabha (Lower House): Maximum 550 elected members (currently 543 elected constituencies); term of 5 years; presided over by the Speaker
Rajya Sabha (Upper House): Permanent house not subject to dissolution; 1/3rd of members retire every 2 years (6-year term); presided over by the Vice President of India as ex-officio Chairman
Three Parliamentary Sessions: Budget Session (Feb–May), Monsoon Session (July–August), Winter Session (Nov–Dec)
Money Bill (Article 110): Can only be introduced in Lok Sabha on President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend, can only delay for 14 days

title: Panchayati Raj & Local Self-Government (NCERT Class 6 & 10)
answer: The Panchayati Raj is India's three-tier system of local rural self-government constitutionally formalized by the 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1992 (adding Part IX and 11th Schedule). The three tiers are Gram Panchayat at the village level, Panchayat Samiti at the block level, and Zilla Parishad at the district level.
highlights: Constitutional Status: 73rd Amendment Act 1992 (came into force on 24 April 1993, celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day)
Three Tiers: 1) Gram Panchayat (Village level, headed by Sarpanch), 2) Panchayat Samiti / Mandal (Block level), 3) Zilla Parishad (District level)
Gram Sabha: General body of all registered voters residing in a village; serves as the cornerstone of grassroots direct democracy
Mandatory Reservation: Minimum 1/3rd (33%) of all seats and chairperson positions reserved for women across all tiers

keywords: supreme court high court subordinate courts
title: Indian Judiciary System — Hierarchy & Powers (NCERT Class 8)
answer: India has a single, integrated, and independent judicial hierarchy with the Supreme Court of India at the apex in New Delhi, followed by High Courts in the States, and Subordinate Courts (District and Sessions Courts) at the base. The Chief Justice of India (CJI) heads the Supreme Court.
highlights: Hierarchy: Supreme Court (Apex court) → High Courts (25 High Courts across Indian states) → Subordinate District/Sessions Courts
Supreme Court Jurisdiction: Original (inter-state disputes, fundamental rights enforcement under Article 32), Appellate (civil and criminal appeals), and Advisory (Article 143 to President)
Judicial Review: Power of Supreme Court and High Courts to strike down legislative statutes or executive actions violating the Constitution (Basic Structure Doctrine - Kesavananda Bharati case 1973)
Public Interest Litigation (PIL): Introduced by Justice P.N. Bhagwati and Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer to democratize access to justice for marginalized citizens

keywords: louis xvi reign of terror robespierre
title: The French Revolution (1789–1799)
answer: The French Revolution began on 14 July 1789 with the Storming of the Bastille fortress prison in Paris, overthrowing the Bourbon monarchy of King Louis XVI. It introduced the revolutionary ideals of Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity (Liberté, égalité, fraternité) to modern democracy.
highlights: Three Estates of Old Regime: Clergy (1st), Nobility (2nd), Commoners (3rd Estate — bore all taxes)
Tennis Court Oath (20 June 1789): National Assembly pledged to write a new Constitution
Reign of Terror (1793–1794): Maximilien Robespierre executed thousands via Guillotine
Ended in 1799 when Napoleon Bonaparte staged a coup d'état and became First Consul

title: The Industrial Revolution (c. 1760 – 1840) (NCERT Class 9 & 10)
answer: The Industrial Revolution was the historic transition from manual, agrarian craftsmanship to mechanized factory-based mass manufacturing, beginning in Great Britain in the late 18th century powered by coal, iron metallurgy, and the steam engine.
highlights: Origin in Britain: Abundant coal/iron ore reserves, capital from colonial trade, patent protections, and transportation networks (canals, railways)
Key Inventions: James Hargreaves (Spinning Jenny 1764), Richard Arkwright (Water Frame 1769), James Watt (Rotary Steam Engine 1769–1776), George Stephenson (Steam Locomotive Rocket 1829)
Social Impact: Massive urbanization, emergence of the working class (proletariat) and industrial capitalism, child labor concerns leading to Factory Acts
Impact on India: De-industrialized traditional Indian handloom textile artisans due to floods of cheap British machine-made cloth

title: Cell Theory — Schleiden, Schwann & Virchow
answer: Cell Theory states: (1) All living organisms are composed of one or more cells, (2) The cell is the basic unit of structure and organisation in organisms, (3) All cells arise from pre-existing cells (Omnis cellula-e-cellula proposed by Rudolf Virchow in 1855).
highlights: Proposed by Matthias Schleiden (1838) and Theodor Schwann (1839)
Rudolf Virchow added 3rd postulate in 1855: cells come from pre-existing cells
Viruses are notable exception to cell theory (acellular)

title: Mitochondria — Powerhouse of the Cell
answer: Mitochondria are known as the powerhouse of the cell because they produce cellular energy in the form of ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate) through aerobic respiration. They possess their own circular DNA and 70S ribosomes, making them semi-autonomous.
highlights: Produces ATP (energy currency of the cell) via oxidative phosphorylation
Has double membrane: outer smooth, inner folded into cristae (increases surface area)
Contains own DNA and ribosomes (maternally inherited in humans)

title: Chloroplast and Plastids in Plant Cells
answer: Chloroplasts are known as the kitchen of the plant cell because they conduct photosynthesis. They contain the green pigment chlorophyll which traps solar energy. Plastids are found only in plant cells: Chloroplasts (green), Chromoplasts (coloured), and Leucoplasts (colourless storage).
highlights: Chloroplasts contain thylakoids arranged in stacks called grana, surrounded by stroma
Chromoplasts give flowers and fruits yellow, orange, and red colours (carotenoids)
Leucoplasts store starch (amyloplasts), oils (elaioplasts), or proteins (aleuroplasts)

title: Nucleus — Control Centre of the Cell
answer: The nucleus is the control centre (brain) of eukaryotic cells, discovered by Robert Brown in 1831. It contains genetic material in the form of chromatin (DNA + histone proteins) and the nucleolus, which synthesizes ribosomal RNA (rRNA).
highlights: Discovered by Robert Brown in 1831 in orchid root cells
Surrounded by double membrane nuclear envelope with nuclear pores
Directs protein synthesis and cell division

title: Endoplasmic Reticulum (RER & SER)
answer: The Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER) is a network of membranous tubules within the cytoplasm. Rough ER (RER) has ribosomes on its surface and synthesizes proteins; Smooth ER (SER) lacks ribosomes and synthesizes lipids, steroids, and detoxifies drugs/poisons in liver cells.
highlights: Rough ER: Protein synthesis and folding with bound 80S ribosomes
Smooth ER: Lipid synthesis, steroid hormone production, and detoxification
Forms skeletal framework of cytoplasm and helps in membrane biogenesis

title: Golgi Apparatus — Packaging and Dispatch Unit
answer: The Golgi apparatus (discovered by Camillo Golgi in 1898) consists of flattened membrane-bound sacs called cisternae. It functions as the post office of the cell by packaging, modifying, and sorting proteins and lipids received from the ER for secretion or intracellular delivery.
highlights: Discovered by Camillo Golgi in 1898 using silver nitrate staining
Two distinct faces: Cis face (forming/receiving) and Trans face (maturing/shipping)
Produces lysosomes and helps in complex sugar synthesis

title: Lysosomes — Suicide Bags of the Cell
answer: Lysosomes are membrane-bound vesicles containing acidic hydrolytic enzymes (optimal pH ~4.5-5.0) capable of breaking down all biological polymers. Discovered by Christian de Duve, they are called suicide bags because if a cell is damaged, lysosomes may burst and digest their own cell.
highlights: Discovered by Christian de Duve in 1955
Contain ~50 hydrolytic enzymes including proteases, lipases, nucleases, and glycosidases
Perform autophagy (eating damaged organelles) and phagocytosis (eating foreign pathogens)

title: Mendel's Laws of Inheritance (Genetics)
answer: Gregor Johann Mendel, the Father of Genetics, formulated the laws of inheritance using garden pea plants (Pisum sativum): (1) Law of Dominance, (2) Law of Segregation (purity of gametes, 3:1 phenotypic ratio in monohybrid cross), and (3) Law of Independent Assortment (9:3:3:1 ratio in dihybrid cross).
highlights: Selected Pisum sativum (garden pea) with 7 pairs of contrasting traits
Monohybrid cross phenotypic ratio: 3:1; Genotypic ratio: 1:2:1
Dihybrid cross phenotypic ratio: 9:3:3:1 (Yellow Round, Yellow Wrinkled, Green Round, Green Wrinkled)

title: Human Eye and Defects of Vision
answer: The human eye works like a camera forming inverted real images on the retina. Cornea refracts light, Iris controls pupil diameter, Ciliary muscles change lens focal length (power of accommodation, near point 25 cm). Myopia (short-sightedness) is corrected with concave lenses; Hypermetropia (far-sightedness) with convex lenses.
highlights: Near point of normal human eye: 25 cm; Far point: Infinity
Retina has Rod cells (night/dim light vision) and Cone cells (colour/daylight vision)
Myopia: Image forms in front of retina; corrected by Concave lens
Hypermetropia: Image forms behind retina; corrected by Convex lens
Presbyopia: Old-age loss of accommodation; corrected by Bifocal lens

title: Dispersion of Light and Rainbow Formation
answer: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its 7 constituent colours (VIBGYOR: Violet, Indigo, Blue, Green, Yellow, Orange, Red) when passing through a glass prism, first demonstrated by Sir Isaac Newton. Red deviates the least (longest wavelength ~700 nm), Violet deviates the most (shortest wavelength ~400 nm).
highlights: VIBGYOR: Violet (max deviation, min wavelength) to Red (min deviation, max wavelength)
Rainbow caused by dispersion, refraction, and internal reflection in spherical raindrops
Atmospheric refraction causes twinkling of stars and advance sunrise/delayed sunset by 2 minutes

title: Types of Chemical Reactions (Class 10)
answer: The five primary chemical reaction types are: (1) Combination: A + B → AB (e.g. CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2), (2) Decomposition: AB → A + B (thermal, electrolytic, or photolytic), (3) Displacement: A + BC → AC + B (e.g. Fe + CuSO4 → FeSO4 + Cu), (4) Double Displacement: AB + CD → AD + CB (precipitation), (5) Redox (simultaneous oxidation and reduction).
highlights: Combination: Exothermic quicklime slaking produces slaked lime
Thermal decomposition: 2FeSO4 (green) → Fe2O3 (brown) + SO2 + SO3
Electrolytic decomposition: 2H2O → 2H2 (cathode) + O2 (anode) in 2:1 volume ratio
Photolytic decomposition: 2AgCl (white) → 2Ag (grey) + Cl2 in sunlight (used in black-and-white photography)

title: Atomic Structure Models — Thomson, Rutherford, Bohr
answer: Atomic models evolved from: (1) Thomson's Plum Pudding model (electrons in positive sphere, 1897), (2) Rutherford's Gold Foil α-particle experiment (1911) discovering the dense positive nucleus, and (3) Bohr's Model (1913) where electrons occupy discrete stationary orbits with quantized angular momentum (L = nh/2π).
highlights: Rutherford's experiment showed most space in atom is empty, with mass concentrated in tiny nucleus
Discovery of subatomic particles: Electron (J.J. Thomson 1897), Proton (Goldstein/Rutherford 1886/1919), Neutron (James Chadwick 1932)
Bohr-Bury scheme: Maximum electrons in nth shell = 2n² (K=2, L=8, M=18, N=32)

title: States of Matter and Phase Transitions
answer: Matter exists in 5 states: Solid (fixed shape and volume), Liquid (fixed volume, variable shape), Gas (variable shape and volume), Plasma (ionized gas at extreme temperatures), and Bose-Einstein Condensate (matter at near absolute zero 0 K).
highlights: Sublimation: Direct transition from solid to gas without liquid phase (e.g. Camphor, Ammonium chloride, Dry Ice)
Deposition: Direct transition from gas to solid
Latent Heat: Heat absorbed/released during phase change without temperature rise
0°C = 273.15 K; Boiling point of water = 100°C = 373.15 K

title: Work, Energy and Power (Class 9)
answer: Work (W) = F · s · cosθ (measured in Joules). Kinetic Energy (KE) = ½mv². Gravitational Potential Energy (PE) = mgh. Law of Conservation of Energy: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted. Power (P) = Work/Time (measured in Watts; 1 HP = 746 W).
highlights: Work is zero if displacement is perpendicular to force (e.g. Earth orbiting Sun)
Work-Energy Theorem: Net work done on an object equals change in its kinetic energy (W = ΔKE)
Commercial unit of energy: 1 kWh = 1 unit = 3.6 × 10⁶ Joules
1 Horsepower (HP) = 746 Watts

title: Sound Waves — Propagation, Echo and SONAR
answer: Sound is a mechanical longitudinal wave requiring a material medium to propagate (cannot travel in vacuum). Speed in air at 20°C is ~343 m/s (fastest in solids, slowest in gases). Echo requires minimum obstacle distance of 17.2 m for distinct hearing. SONAR uses ultrasonic sound waves to measure underwater depths.
highlights: Audible range for human ear: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz)
Infrasound (<20 Hz): Elephants, whales, earthquakes; Ultrasound (>20 kHz): Bats, dolphins, SONAR, echocardiography
Echo minimum distance = (v × t)/2 = (344 m/s × 0.1 s)/2 = 17.2 metres
SONAR: Sound Navigation and Ranging (Distance d = (v × t) / 2)

title: Indus Valley Civilization (Bronze Age 2500–1900 BCE)
answer: The Indus Valley Civilization (Harappan Civilization, ~2500–1900 BCE) was a Bronze Age urban civilization known for grid-plan cities, advanced covered drainage systems, standardized baked bricks, and maritime trade. Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni (1921) and Mohenjo-daro by R.D. Banerjee (1922).
highlights: Key sites: Harappa (Ravi river, Pakistan), Mohenjo-daro (Indus, Great Bath & Granary), Lothal (Gujarat, dockyard/port), Kalibangan (Rajasthan, ploughed fields)
Script: Boustrophedon / pictographic (undeciphered till date)
Bronze Dancing Girl and Steatite Bearded Priest found at Mohenjo-daro
Declined ~1900 BCE likely due to climate shift, drying of Saraswati river, and floods

title: Buddhism and Jainism — 6th Century BCE Sramana Traditions
answer: Buddhism was founded by Siddhartha Gautama (Lord Buddha, 563–483 BCE) who attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya and taught Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path (Ashtangika Marga). Jainism was systematized by Vardhamana Mahavira (24th Tirthankara, 599–527 BCE) emphasizing Ahimsa (non-violence) and Anekantavada.
highlights: Buddha: First sermon at Sarnath (Dhammacakkappavattana); Parinirvana at Kushinagar; Tripitakas (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma)
Four Buddhist Councils: Rajgriha (483 BCE), Vaishali (383 BCE), Pataliputra (250 BCE under Ashoka), Kundalvana (72 CE under Kanishka)
Mahavira: 24th Tirthankara; Three Jewels (Triratna): Right Faith, Right Knowledge, Right Conduct
Two main sects: Buddhism (Hinayana, Mahayana); Jainism (Digambara, Svetambara)

title: Russian Revolution of 1917 and Rise of the USSR
answer: The Russian Revolution of 1917 consisted of the February Revolution (overthrew Tsar Nicholas II and Romanov dynasty) and the October Revolution led by Vladimir Lenin and the Bolsheviks, establishing the world's first communist state which became the USSR (Soviet Union) in 1922.
highlights: February 1917: Food shortages and WWI losses forced Tsar Nicholas II to abdicate
October 1917: Lenin's Bolsheviks seized power with slogan "Peace, Land, and Bread"
April Theses: Lenin's program to end war, transfer land to peasants, and nationalize banks
Civil War (Reds vs Whites) ended in 1922 with the formation of the USSR under Bolshevik rule

title: Rise of Nationalism in Europe and Unifications
answer: Nationalism in 19th-century Europe transformed multi-ethnic empires into modern nation-states. Key milestones: Unification of Germany (1871 under Otto von Bismarck via "Blood and Iron" policy) and Unification of Italy (1861 led by Giuseppe Mazzini, Count Cavour, and Giuseppe Garibaldi).
highlights: Treaty of Vienna (1815): Restored Bourbon monarchy under conservative order after Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo
Giuseppe Mazzini founded secret society "Young Italy" in Marseilles in 1831
Otto von Bismarck orchestrated three wars (against Denmark, Austria, and France) to unify Germany in 1871
Kaiser Wilhelm I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles (1871)

title: Preamble and Architecture of Indian Constitution
answer: The Preamble is the introductory statement of the Constitution of India declaring India a "Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic" securing Justice, Liberty, Equality, and Fraternity. Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was Chairman of the Drafting Committee. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and enacted on 26 January 1950.
highlights: Key words added by 42nd Amendment (1976): "Socialist", "Secular", and "Integrity"
Constituent Assembly took 2 years, 11 months, and 18 days to draft the Constitution
Adopted 26 November 1949 (National Constitution Day); In effect from 26 January 1950 (Republic Day)
Dr. B.R. Ambedkar regarded Article 32 (Constitutional Remedies) as the Heart and Soul of the Constitution

title: Power Sharing and Federalism (Civics Class 10)
answer: Federalism is a system of government where power is divided between a central authority and constituent units (States). India has a 3-tier federal system (Union, State, Local Panchayati Raj) with legislative powers divided into Union List (100 items), State List (61 items), and Concurrent List (52 items).
highlights: Union List: Defence, Foreign Affairs, Banking, Currency (Union Parliament only)
State List: Police, Public Health, Agriculture, Prisons (State Legislature)
Concurrent List: Education, Forests, Marriage, Trade Unions (Both make laws; Union prevails in conflict)
Residuary Powers (e.g. Cyber Law) vest exclusively with the Union Parliament in India (Article 248)

title: Climate of India and the South-West Monsoon
answer: India has a tropical monsoon climate dominated by seasonal reversal of winds. The South-West Monsoon arrives in Kerala around 1 June and covers the entire subcontinent by mid-July, providing over 75% of India's annual rainfall across two branches: Arabian Sea branch and Bay of Bengal branch.
highlights: Onset: 1 June in Kerala; retreats starting September from NW India
Mawsynram in Meghalaya receives the highest average annual rainfall in the world (~11,872 mm)
Western Disturbances: Cyclonic storms from Mediterranean bring winter rain to NW India (vital for Rabi wheat crop)
El Niño causes weak monsoons/droughts in India; La Niña brings normal to excess rainfall

title: Newton's Three Laws of Motion & Momentum Conservation (Class 9)
answer: Sir Isaac Newton formulated 3 laws of motion: (1) First Law (Inertia): An object remains at rest or uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an external net force. (2) Second Law: Force F = dp/dt = ma (rate of change of momentum is proportional to applied force). (3) Third Law: To every action there is an equal and opposite reaction (F_AB = -F_BA). Law of Conservation of Momentum: Total momentum before collision equals total momentum after collision (m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂).
highlights: First Law defines Inertia (mass is quantitative measure of inertia)
Second Law gives mathematical definition and unit of Force: 1 Newton = 1 kg·m/s²
Third Law explains rocket propulsion, recoiling of gun, and walking
Momentum p = mv (vector quantity with SI unit kg·m/s)
Impulse J = F · Δt = Change in momentum (Δp)

title: Archimedes' Principle, Buoyancy & Relative Density (Class 9)
answer: Archimedes' Principle states that when an object is immersed fully or partially in a fluid, it experiences an upward buoyant force (upthrust) equal to the weight of the fluid displaced: F_b = ρ_fluid · V_displaced · g. Relative Density = Density of substance / Density of water at 4°C (dimensionless ratio).
highlights: Buoyant force F_b = V · ρ · g (acts upward through center of buoyancy)
Law of Floatation: An object floats if buoyant force equals its total weight (or if density < fluid density)
Lactometers (milk purity) and Hydrometers (liquid density) are built on Archimedes' principle
Relative density of iron ~7.8, gold ~19.3, water = 1.0 (substances with RD > 1 sink in water; RD < 1 float)

title: The Mole Concept and Avogadro's Number (Class 9 & 11)
answer: A mole is the amount of substance containing exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities (Avogadro's Constant N_A). Formulas: (1) Number of moles n = Mass (m) / Molar Mass (M), (2) Number of particles N = n · N_A = (m/M) · N_A, (3) Volume of 1 mole of any ideal gas at STP (Standard Temperature and Pressure: 0°C, 1 atm) is 22.4 Litres (or 22.7 L at 1 bar).
highlights: Avogadro Constant: N_A = 6.022 × 10²³ particles/mol
1 mole of Carbon-12 has a mass of exactly 12 grams
Molar volume of ideal gas at STP (273.15 K, 1 atm) = 22.4 L/mol
Percentage composition = (Mass of element in 1 mole of compound / Molar mass of compound) × 100%

title: Human Excretory System and Nephron Physiology (Class 10)
answer: The human excretory system consists of a pair of kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder, and urethra. The Nephron is the structural and functional filtration unit of the kidney (~1 million nephrons per kidney). Urine formation occurs in 3 steps: (1) Ultrafiltration in Glomerulus into Bowman's capsule (GFR ~125 mL/min or 180 L/day), (2) Selective Reabsorption along Proximal Convoluted Tubule (PCT) and Loop of Henle (reabsorbing glucose, amino acids, salts, 99% of water), (3) Tubular Secretion in Distal Convoluted Tubule (DCT) releasing K+, H+, and ammonia into urine (~1.5 L/day produced).
highlights: Glomerulus + Bowman's Capsule = Malpighian Body / Renal Corpuscle
Selective Reabsorption: PCT reabsorbs 70–80% of electrolytes and water
Loop of Henle (descending limb permeable to water; ascending limb permeable to electrolytes) maintains hyperosmolarity
Hemodialysis (artificial kidney) removes nitrogenous metabolic waste (urea, creatinine) across semipermeable cellophane membranes

title: Plant Hormones (Phytohormones) and Tropic Movements (Class 10)
answer: Plant growth and responses are regulated by 5 major classes of Phytohormones: (1) Auxins (cell elongation, phototropism, apical dominance), (2) Gibberellins (stem elongation, breaking seed dormancy, bolting), (3) Cytokinins (cell division promotion, delaying senescence), (4) Abscisic Acid / ABA (growth inhibitor, stress hormone, stomatal closure during drought, leaf abscission), and (5) Ethylene (only gaseous plant hormone, promotes fruit ripening). Tropic movements: Phototropism (light), Geotropism (gravity), Hydrotropism (water), Chemotropism (pollen tube growth towards ovule), Thigmotropism (touch response in tendrils).
highlights: Auxin: Synthesized at shoot tips; diffuses to shaded side causing cells to elongate faster, bending shoot toward light
Gibberellin: Induces internode elongation in rosette plants (bolting)
Cytokinins: Promote rapid cell division in fruits, seeds, and root tips; counteracts apical dominance
Abscisic Acid (ABA): Stress hormone closing stomata under water deficit
Ethylene (C₂H₄): Gaseous hormone accelerating fruit ripening and flower fading

title: Human Heart, Double Circulation & Cardiac Cycle (Class 10 & 11)
answer: The human heart is myogenic, regulated by the SA (Sinoatrial) Node ("natural pacemaker" generating 70–75 action potentials/min in right atrium). Double Circulation comprises Pulmonary Circulation (Right Ventricle → Pulmonary Artery → Lungs → Pulmonary Vein → Left Atrium) and Systemic Circulation (Left Ventricle → Aorta → Body Tissues → Vena Cava → Right Atrium). The Cardiac Cycle lasts 0.8 seconds (Atrial Systole 0.1s, Ventricular Systole 0.3s, Joint Diastole 0.4s).
highlights: Pacemaker pathway: SA Node → AV (Atrioventricular) Node → Bundle of His → Purkinje Fibers
Cardiac output = Stroke Volume (~70 mL) × Heart Rate (~72 bpm) ≈ 5.0 Litres/minute
Heart Sounds: "LUB" (closure of tricuspid and bicuspid/mitral valves) and "DUB" (closure of semilunar valves)
ECG Waves: P-wave (Atrial depolarization), QRS-complex (Ventricular depolarization), T-wave (Ventricular repolarization)
Coronary arteries supply oxygenated blood directly to cardiac muscle tissue

title: Allotropes of Carbon — Diamond, Graphite, Fullerenes & Graphene
answer: Carbon exhibits allotropy in crystalline forms: (1) Diamond (each C atom is sp³ hybridized and tetrahedrally bonded to 4 other C atoms in a rigid 3D lattice, hardest natural substance, electrical insulator, refractive index 2.42), (2) Graphite (each C atom is sp² hybridized, bonded to 3 C atoms forming hexagonal layers held by weak van der Waals forces, free π-electrons make it a good conductor, soft and slippery lubricant), (3) Buckminsterfullerene C₆₀ (spherical cage of 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons like a football), (4) Graphene (single 2D atomic layer of sp² carbon with record tensile strength and electrical mobility).
highlights: Diamond: sp³ hybridization, bond length 1.54 Å, no free electrons (electrical insulator), thermal conductor
Graphite: sp² hybridization, planar hexagonal sheets with delocalized π-electrons (conducts electricity), layer spacing 3.35 Å
Fullerenes (C₆₀): Discovered by Kroto, Curl, and Smalley (1996 Nobel Prize)
Graphene: Discovered by Geim and Novoselov (2010 Nobel Prize); 200× stronger than steel and ballistic conductor

title: Detailed Periodic Table Trends & Anomalies (Class 10 & 11)
answer: Across a Period (Left to Right): Atomic radius decreases, Effective nuclear charge (Z_eff) increases, Ionization Enthalpy increases (with anomalies: N > O due to half-filled 2p³ stability, and Be > B due to fully-filled 2s² stability), Electronegativity increases, Non-metallic character increases. Down a Group (Top to Bottom): Atomic radius increases, Screening/shielding effect increases, Ionization Enthalpy decreases, Metallic character increases, Electropositivity increases.
highlights: Atomic Radii decrease across period due to increasing nuclear attraction pulling outer electrons inward
Ionization Enthalpy exception: Nitrogen (1402 kJ/mol) has higher IE than Oxygen (1314 kJ/mol) due to extra stability of half-filled 2p³ subshell
Electron Gain Enthalpy exception: Chlorine (-349 kJ/mol) is more negative than Fluorine (-328 kJ/mol) because F has small 2p orbital causing strong inter-electronic repulsion
Diagonal Relationships: Lithium-Magnesium, Beryllium-Aluminum, and Boron-Silicon share similar ionic size and charge density
